prompt.context: Our client, Vitality Insurance, is a leading provider of supplemental insurance products in the United States. Vitality agents partner with companies to offer their employees optional, supplemental insurance for such conditions as life, long-term disability, etc. Vitality has undergone fairly steady growth in the past two years, but profit margin is decreasing.
prompt.question: What should Vitality do about its declining profit margin?

clarifying_info.q: How many agents does Vitality have?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality is the leader in its category and has over 10,000 field sales agents.
Agents are solely compensated on a percentage commission of total new premium, defined as premium from new customers or additional premium (up-sell) from existing policyholders.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any additional incentives beyond base commission?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. In addition to commission, short-term priorities are often communicated via sales contests that focus on a particular customer segment or activity and pay a bonus in addition to standard commission.

clarifying_info.q: What are the major cost categories?
clarifying_info.a: Major costs are sales, G&A (General and Administrative), and advertising.
Vitality has a few competitors who have seen similar growth, but Vitality is the leader in the space and competition is not the focus.
It is a mature market. Agent turnover is very high on a yearly basis, though it was lower during the recessionary period.

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Key Results and Costs
exhibits.shows: A table of Vitality's key results and cost line items for 2008, 2009, and 2010 (figures in $000s).

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Sales Process and Contest Mix
exhibits.shows: A diagram of Vitality's selling process steps (Hire new agents, Acquire new accounts, Keep accounts active, Upsell active accounts, Produce results/Premium $, Reactivating dormant account) with a table showing the number of sales contests targeted at each step by year (2008, 2009, 2010).

exhibits.title: Snapshot of Sweeps Week Contest Results
exhibits.shows: A line chart showing weekly premium (as a ratio to average weekly premium 2008-2010) for weeks 1-27 (January-June) across years 2008, 2009, and 2010, with two 'Sweeps Week' contests in 2010 marked at approximately weeks 4 and 20.

data.y_axis: Ratio to Average Weekly Premium (2008-2010), 0% to 200%
data.observation: 2010 line spikes sharply upward at Sweeps Week weeks, with surrounding weeks appearing depressed relative to 2008/2009 baselines

framework: Profitability = Revenue - Costs; investigate both sides
Revenue: examine premium growth trends (accounts, policyholders, premium per policyholder)
Costs: break down into G&A, Sales, Advertising; identify which cost line is growing anomalously
Sales costs deep dive: understand commission structure and sales contest mechanics
Sales contest mix: compare contest focus and volume across 2008, 2009, 2010
Evaluate contest effectiveness: are increased sales costs generating incremental premium?
Identify specific problematic contest(s) and diagnose root cause behavior
Recommendation: modify or eliminate ineffective contests; redirect spend

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, what do you observe about Vitality's revenue and cost trends from 2008 to 2010?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates identify: (1) Revenue (premium) grows at ~10% per year consistently ($2.5M -> $2.75M -> $3.025M). (2) G&A and Advertising also grow ~10% per year (in line with revenue). (3) Sales costs grow 10% from 2008 to 2009 ($250K -> $275K), but jump 45% from 2009 to 2010 ($275K -> $400K) — far outpacing premium growth of 10%. (4) Profit margin declines from 9.5% to 9.4% to 8.5%, with the steepest drop in 2010. The anomaly is the 2010 sales cost spike.

math.setup: Sales cost growth rates and profit margin verification
steps: Excess sales cost in 2010 vs. 10% growth baseline: Expected sales cost at 10% growth = $275K * 1.10 = $302.5K; Actual = $400K; Excess = $400K - $302.5K = $97.5K

Profit margin 2010: Revenue = $3,025,000K; Total costs = $58K + $400K + $30K = $488K (in $000s); but note figures — premium is in $000s at $3,025,000 means $3.025B; costs sum = $488K (000s). Margin given directly as 8.50%.
math.answer: Sales costs grew ~45% in 2010 vs. 10% premium growth. Excess sales cost above trend is ~$97,500 (in $000s). Profit margin dropped 90 basis points from 2009 to 2010, driven by the sales cost overrun.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 2, what changed in Vitality's sales contest mix from 2008/2009 to 2010?
questions.guidance: Candidates should identify two key shifts: (1) Contests focused on 'Keep accounts active' dropped from 4 to 0 — Vitality stopped incentivizing retention of existing accounts. (2) Contests focused on 'Acquire new accounts' doubled from 2 to 4 and contests focused on 'Produce results (total premium $)' doubled from 2 to 4. The 2010 mix heavily emphasizes new account acquisition and total premium volume, de-emphasizing account retention. Strong candidates note that new account acquisition is more expensive than retaining or upselling existing customers, so this shift likely hurts margins further.

questions.prompt: You are told that one of the new 2010 premium-focused contests was called 'Sweeps Week' — Vitality paid an extra 10% bonus on all premium booked in two specific low-volume weeks. Looking at Exhibit 3, evaluate whether Sweeps Week achieved its objective.
questions.guidance: The exhibit shows that in weeks 4 and 20 (the Sweeps Week periods), 2010 premium spikes dramatically relative to the 2008/2009 baseline — reaching ~150-200% of average weekly premium. However, the weeks immediately surrounding each Sweeps Week show depressed premium well below the 2008/2009 baseline. This pattern strongly suggests agents are 'gaming' the contest: they have authority to influence enrollment timing by up to one week, so they pull forward or push back sales into the Sweeps Week to earn the extra 10% bonus. The net new premium generated is minimal or zero — it is the same premium shifted in time. Sweeps Week therefore costs Vitality the 10% bonus without generating incremental premium, making it purely value-destructive.

math.setup: Estimate incremental cost of Sweeps Week bonus vs. incremental premium generated
steps: If agents simply shift existing sales into Sweeps Week with no net new premium, incremental premium = $0
Vitality pays 10% bonus on all premium booked in those two weeks
If, say, $X in premium is booked during Sweeps Weeks, bonus cost = 0.10 * $X with no offsetting new revenue
This is a direct reduction in profit margin
math.answer: Sweeps Week generated no meaningful net new premium (sales were shifted, not created), while incurring an extra 10% bonus cost on booked premium — a net loss for Vitality.

brainstorming.prompt: What other actions could Vitality take to improve profitability beyond eliminating Sweeps Week?

categories.name: Sales contest redesign
ideas: Design contests that incentivize activities not already covered by the base commission (e.g., account retention, cross-sell of new product lines)
Shift contest focus back to keeping accounts active (was 4 contests in 2008/09, 0 in 2010)
Introduce contests with verifiable new-premium conditions (e.g., bonus only if net new accounts exceed baseline)
Use multi-week or quarterly measurement periods to prevent gaming

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Reduce advertising spend if agents are the primary distribution channel
Renegotiate G&A vendors or find shared-service efficiencies
Reduce agent turnover to lower recruiting/training costs (high turnover is noted as a structural issue)

categories.name: Revenue enhancement
ideas: Up-sell existing policyholders on additional coverage (already incentivized but contest support dropped to 1)
Reactivate dormant accounts — currently appears uncontested in 2010
Expand into adjacent supplemental insurance products to increase premium per policyholder
Target higher-value employer groups to increase average premium

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Review premium pricing relative to claims experience
Segment pricing by risk profile to improve underwriting margins

recommendation: Eliminate the 'Sweeps Week' contest immediately — it incentivizes agents to game enrollment timing rather than generate net new premium, and adds a 10% bonus cost with no incremental revenue benefit

Restore contests focused on keeping accounts active (dropped from 4 to 0 in 2010) to improve retention economics, since retaining or up-selling an existing customer is far cheaper than acquiring a new one

Evaluate the two new 'acquire new accounts' contests with caution — new account acquisition is inherently more expensive and margin-dilutive; any such contest should be benchmarked against the lifetime value of the accounts acquired
risks: Eliminating Sweeps Week may cause short-term agent dissatisfaction if it was popular; communication and change management needed
Shifting contest focus back to retention may slow new account growth, which could be a strategic priority leadership has not disclosed
Agent turnover (structurally high) may worsen if perceived contest value drops, increasing recruiting costs
next_steps: Quantify the full P&L impact of Sweeps Week (total bonus paid in 2010 vs. net new premium generated)
Audit the other new 2010 contests (new account bonuses) to assess whether incremental account acquisition justifies the added cost
Redesign the 2011 contest calendar with a balanced mix: retain accounts, upsell existing, and carefully incentivize net-new premium only where it is truly incremental
Model agent lifetime value and customer lifetime value to better calibrate commission and contest economics going forward
